title_en: ProSAAS overexpression arrests progression of motor deficits in a rat alpha-synuclein model of Parkinson's disease.
title_zh: ProSAAS overexpression arrests progression of motor deficits in a rat alpha-synuclein model of Parkinson's disease.

title_en: Regulating the iron-ROS cycle via electronic structure-engineered nanoregulators for Parkinson's disease therapy.
title_zh: Regulating the iron-ROS cycle via electronic structure-engineered nanoregulators for Parkinson's disease therapy.
abstract: Iron-driven reactive oxygen species (ROS) amplification forms a self-sustaining pathological cycle in Parkinson's disease (PD), yet remains difficult to therapeutically interrupt due to the lack of strategies that coordinate metal homeostasis and redox regulation. Here, we report an electronic-structure-engineered nanoregulatory strategy that regulates the iron-ROS cycle rather than passively scavenging ROS. Nitrogen-doped, herbal-derived carbon dots (CD) were rationally constructed to establish a conjugated electronic framework, in which heteroatom-induced electron delocalization defined redox-active sites and governed the coupling between iron chelation and catalytic ROS regulation. This structure-electronic state-function relationship enabled programmable disruption of the iron-ROS feedback loop at its source. Functionally, the nanoregulators achieved low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 1 (LRP1)-mediated brain delivery, exhibited efficient central nervous system exposure, and underwent brain clearance via the cerebrospinal fluid pathway. At the cellular level, they restored mitochondrial function, suppressed ferroptosis-associated lipid peroxidation, and reprogramed stress-related pathways toward neuronal survival. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed coordinated regulation of redox, metabolic, and inflammatory networks. In Parkinsonian mice, this strategy reduced iron deposition, preserved dopaminergic neurons, and improved motor function. Integration with levodopa further enabled sustained, disease-modifying neuroprotection.

title_en: Harnessing cGAS-STING in neurodegeneration: From mitochondrial DNA leakage and microglial reactivity to species-specific translational barriers.
title_zh: Harnessing cGAS-STING in neurodegeneration: From mitochondrial DNA leakage and microglial reactivity to species-specific translational barriers.
abstract: The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) pathway, a cornerstone of innate immunity, has emerged as a critical driver of sterile neuroinflammation in the aging brain. Age-related decline in mitochondrial quality control, coupled with nuclear and lysosomal erosion, fosters the aberrant accumulation of cytosolic self-DNA, establishing a permissive environment for chronic cGAS-STING activation. This review synthesizes recent breakthroughs elucidating how major neurodegenerative diseases-Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and Huntington's disease-converge on this pathway through distinct, disease-specific triggers, ranging from PINK1/Parkin deficiency-driven mitochondrial DNA leakage to TDP-43 proteinopathy-associated retrotransposon de-repression. Critically, we evaluate the translational landscape, highlighting the profound challenge posed by species-specific pharmacology, as exemplified by the failure of the covalent inhibitor H-151 to engage human STING. We argue that the future of therapeutic intervention lies not in wholesale pathway ablation, but in nuanced, context-dependent fine-tuning that disentangles its detrimental chronic effects from its indispensable homeostatic functions. This review positions the cGAS-STING axis as a promising yet delicate frontier for combating age-related neurodegeneration.

title_en: TGF-beta Inhibition Attenuates Tau Accumulation and Neurodegeneration in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy Patient-Derived Organoids.
title_zh: TGF-beta Inhibition Attenuates Tau Accumulation and Neurodegeneration in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy Patient-Derived Organoids.
journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
abstract: BACKGROUND: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a devastating 4-repeat tauopathy with no approved disease-modifying treatments. Recent evidence showed increased transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) levels in PSP patient-derived ventral midbrain organoids (vMOs) and serum neuronally derived exosomes. OBJECTIVE: This study investigated whether TGF-beta pharmacological inhibition could mitigate PSP pathology in vMOs. METHODS: Ninety-six vMOs were generated from induced pluripotent stem cells from two PSP-Richardson's syndrome patients and two healthy control donors (HCs). From day 60 to day 90, PSP organoids were (1) exposed to TGF-beta receptor I inhibitor (SB431542); (2) exposed to recombinant TGF-beta1, TGF-beta2, and TGF-beta3; or (3) untreated. At day 90, several tau species were assessed by immunoblotting; neurodegeneration was evaluated through TUNEL assay and immunofluorescence (tyrosine hydroxylase [TH], neurofilament light chain [NfL]); astrocytic activation (glial fibrillary acidic protein [GFAP]) marker was evaluated by immunofluorescence, and histopathological hallmarks were evaluated by immunohistochemistry. An HC-derived organoid subgroup was exposed to the treatment conditions to assess potential toxicity. RESULTS: At day 90, untreated PSP-derived vMOs exhibited increased phosphorylated tau levels (Ser396, Thr181, Ser202/Ser205 [AT8]) compared with HC-derived vMOs, dopaminergic neuron loss (reduced TH, increased NfL), and astrocytic reactivity (increased GFAP), along with PSP characteristic tau deposition. Tau hyperphosphorylation, neurodegeneration, and astrocytic reactivity were all markedly reduced in PSP-derived vMOs treated with TGF-beta receptor I inhibitor. Conversely, exposure to TGF-beta exacerbated these features. No toxic effects were observed in HC vMOs exposed to treatment conditions. CONCLUSIONS: Pharmacological inhibition of TGF-beta signaling prevented key PSP molecular alterations in patient-derived organoids. These findings support further research and pave the way for future investigation of TGF-beta-targeting strategies in clinical trials in patients with PSP. (c) 2026 The Author(s). title_en: Habitual Diet, Gut Microbiome Dysbiosis, and alpha-Synucleinopathy Conversion in Isolated Rapid Eye Movement (REM) Sleep Behavior Disorder.
title_zh: Habitual Diet, Gut Microbiome Dysbiosis, and alpha-Synucleinopathy Conversion in Isolated Rapid Eye Movement (REM) Sleep Behavior Disorder.
journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
abstract: BACKGROUND: Accumulating evidence indicates that habitual diet, including plant-based dietary patterns, is associated with neurodegenerative alpha-synucleinopathy risk. However, the role of diet and its correlation with the gut microbiome in prodromal alpha-synucleinopathy, specifically among patients with isolated rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (iRBD), remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate dietary patterns, their interplay with gut microbial dysbiosis, and longitudinal effects on neurodegenerative progression in iRBD patients. METHODS: We recruited 287 iRBD patients and 208 age- and sex-matched controls. Plant-based diet indices (PDIs) were derived from food frequency questionnaires. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was performed in 456 subjects for diet-microbiome analyses. After a median follow-up of 4.2 years, 45 (15.7%) iRBD patients converted to alpha-synucleinopathies. Cox proportional hazards models assessed the associations between diet and neurodegenerative outcomes. RESULTS: We found that iRBD patients exhibited lower healthful PDIs (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 95% confidence interval [95% CI]: 0.48 [0.29-0.80], P = 0.005) but higher consumption of unhealthful plant-based foods (refined grains, sweets, and sweeteners). Diet-microbiome interaction analysis identified dietary associations for 84.3% of iRBD-related gut microbes, including co-occurrence between healthful PDI and Clostridium sp. AF20-17LB. Longitudinally, four dietary factors and five iRBD-related microbes were associated with neurodegenerative outcomes; specifically, higher coffee consumption was linked to a lower risk of progression to alpha-synucleinopathy (aHR [95% CI]: 0.30 [0.11-0.78], P = 0.01). Furthermore, mediation analyses indicated that the iRBD-enriched species Ruthenibacterium lactatiformans mediated the association between unhealthful PDI and dementia-first conversion. CONCLUSIONS: Habitual diet in iRBD is associated with gut microbiome dysbiosis and predicts neurodegenerative progression. These findings highlight diet-microbiome interactions as modifiable targets for intervention in prodromal alpha-synucleinopathy. (c) 2026 The Author(s). title_en: Automated Quantification of Parkinsonian Facial Expressions via a Transformer-Based Multi-View Multimodal Fusion Framework.
title_zh: Automated Quantification of Parkinsonian Facial Expressions via a Transformer-Based Multi-View Multimodal Fusion Framework.
journal: IEEE journal of biomedical and health informatics
abstract: Facial hypomimia, a common symptom of Parkinson's disease (PD), is characterized by reduced facial expressiveness due to muscle rigidity. Its clinical assessment, typically based on the Movement Disorder Society-Unified PD Rating Scale, is challenging due to the limited clinician availability, subjectivity, and time consuming procedures. In this paper, we propose a transformer-based multi-view multimodal fusion framework for efficient and objective video-based automated assessment of PD facial expressions. The framework incorporates facial anatomical priors, jointly models global and local features, and progressively fuses complementary information across modalities. It uses a progressive fusion strategy for cross-modal interaction and compensation, together with a spatial-temporal transformer block for anatomically guided landmark modeling of global motion and local subtle dynamics. Our proposed method achieved an accuracy of 68.28% and an acceptable accuracy of 87.75% on the largest clinical dataset (637 videos from 354 PD patients) with four classes. Moreover, testing on an independent dataset from another hospital provides preliminary evidence of the model's cross-center transferability, and the framework was further evaluated on two additional medical facial assessment tasks of stroke facial palsy and facial function. In summary, the proposed framework provides an efficient and reliable solution for the objective assessment of PD facial expressions, with the potential to improve evaluation consistency and support broader clinical applications.
